prop: As the refuter on `fact`, Jev performs within the range of the two LLM refuters measured on the same 16 adjudicated `contradicts` findings, at under a hundredth of their cost: Jev (3-draw majority) keeps 8 of 10 true catches at 80% precision, against Sonnet's 8 of 10 at 89% and Gemini's 10 of 10 at 77%; one Jev draw cost $0.0018 for all 16 findings (README: $0.00011 a finding, against $0.0228 and $0.0184), with a median latency of 0.69 seconds.

Jev cannot perform the check leg. The check leg's product is a list of `Finding`s, each with a `clause` meant to quote the author and a quoted evidence span, returned as text by an OpenAI-style chat call. The response TypeSafe's endpoint returned to a request carrying one of each question type had exactly three top-level keys, `answers`, `model` and `usage`, and each answer was an object carrying a probability, a choice among the request's own keys, or a score index, with its probabilities; the only text in it was the resolved model name, the question type names and the request's own labels echoed back. Nothing in that shape can carry a clause, a reason or a quotation, so every design below keeps an LLM on OpenRouter for the check leg and gives Jev only legs whose answer is a choice.

findings.why: The captured implementation constructs the check prompt, calls the provider with the check system prompt, and parses the response into findings, showing that Jev can perform the check leg.

prop: A Jev gate in front of the check leg is worth having on `fact` and `claim` but not on `prose`, and what makes it worth having is asking which unit disagrees rather than whether anything does. prop: Decision — routing and credential. A model value whose vendor half is exactly `typesafe` is sent to TypeSafe's endpoint (a second constant beside `ENDPOINT`, https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone) with a credential read only from the environment variable TYPESAFE_API_KEY, on the same terms `KEY_VARS` states for OpenRouter's: never a config key, never written. Every other value keeps going to OpenRouter unchanged. `is_model_name` already accepts `typesafe/jev-1.13.0`, so the routing needs no new value syntax. `verify.model` refuses a `typesafe/` value at `config set`, through a new `Accepts` variant, because the check leg must be an LLM and a refusal at `config set` can never suppress a mint, where a refusal at mint time would.

Each typed leg ships with the presentation it was measured with, including its splitter, because the numbers belong to the presentation and not to the model. The `fact` gate (`pick_cls`) splits into sentences, asks one `choice` over them plus NONE and one CURRENT/PROPOSED/ARGUMENT `choice` per sentence, and scores the sum of each sentence's pick probability times its P(CURRENT). The `claim` gate (`pick_clause`) cuts every sentence at every `,` `;` `:` or dash, with no bracket awareness, asks one `choice` over the clauses plus NONE, and scores 1 - P(NONE). Jev classify on `claim` cuts clauses only outside brackets and code spans. Both gates put the subject's text before its evidence; both carry NOT_A_DISAGREEMENT, ported from CHECK_SYSTEM, in NONE's criterion. A port that "improves" any of these — one splitter for both, a shared score — is an unmeasured configuration.

findings.evidence: CLAUSE = re.compile(r"(?:,|;|:| —| –)\s+")
findings.why: The captured splitter matches commas, semicolons, colons, and only spaced em/en dashes followed by whitespace; it does not cut at every dash or at these delimiters when they are not followed by whitespace.

prop: Decision — what the gate does to a verification. The gate asks its question first, of the subject's text and evidence alone, before any classify call, which is how it was measured. Below the verb's threshold, no classify and no check call is made and the verification reports a new status, `gated`, never `ok` with an empty findings list: `Status` exists so that nothing empty passes for a clean result. The literal leg, when on, still runs on a gated subject, since it answers a different question and the measured join shows literals-always-run at 20 of 50 needed-work claims flagged against 19 with literals gated, both at 4 of 38 sound. A gate that fails — transport, timeout, an unreadable reply — never skips: the check runs, and the response carries `gate_incomplete` the way it carries `literals_incomplete` today. The gate's probability is never shown to the author; `Finding` carries no confidence score by design, and a verification should not either.

prop: Decision — the refuter. `verify.refuter_model` accepts a `typesafe/` value, answered as one `choice` over CORRECT, WRONG and UNCLEAR with REFUTE_SYSTEM's own criteria, the measured port; only WRONG drops, unchanged. The default refuter stays the LLM it is: Jev's refuter numbers cover `fact`'s `contradicts` findings only. The self-refutation guard in `refute_findings`, which today compares the refuter only against `verify.model`, extends to `verify.typed_model`: when both name the same model, the refuter is not run over `unevidenced` findings that model judged, and `tel.detail` says so as the existing branch does. prop: Each typed leg ships with the presentation it was measured with, including its splitter, because the numbers belong to the presentation and not to the model. The `fact` gate (`pick_cls`) splits into sentences, asks one `choice` over them plus NONE and one CURRENT/PROPOSED/ARGUMENT `choice` per sentence, and scores the sum of each sentence's pick probability times its P(CURRENT). The `claim` gate (`pick_clause`) cuts every sentence at every `,` `;` `:` or dash, with no bracket awareness, asks one `choice` over the clauses plus NONE, and scores 1 - P(NONE). Jev classify on `claim` cuts clauses only outside brackets and code spans. Both gates put the subject's text before its evidence; both carry NOT_A_DISAGREEMENT, ported from CHECK_SYSTEM, in NONE's criterion. A port that "improves" any of these — one splitter for both, a shared score — is an unmeasured configuration.

findings.clause: The `claim` gate (`pick_clause`) cuts every sentence at every `,` `;` `:` or dash, with no bracket awareness
findings.evidence: CLAUSE = re.compile(r"(?:,|;|:| —| –)\s+")
findings.why: The splitter cuts only when the delimiter is followed by whitespace, and recognizes only spaced em/en dashes (`—` and `–`), not every comma, semicolon, colon, or dash.

The non-determinism of this check is measured, not merely theoretical, and the disclosure must be carried in the surface rather than left in documentation. The eval recorded that on identical input at temperature 0 the model's reasoning length swings 516..2000 tokens, and that draws reaching the token cap return `finish_reason=length` with content of length zero — so identical mints can produce different `verify` payloads, including a finding on one run and silence on the next. This is a real departure from `attention` and `overlap`, which are derived per call from workspace state already on disk and therefore repeat exactly. The `verify` object must therefore state its own model and a `deterministic: false` marker in every response, so a reader cannot infer parity with the two findings sitting beside it.

The warning should be carried as a top-level `verify` OBJECT in the mint result, not a fourth array beside `attention` and `overlap`. `mcp.rs` establishes the array form for a reason that holds here — "the caller is a program, and a field it can branch on beats a string it has to notice" — but `attention` and `overlap` are derived per call from workspace state already on disk, so empty and absent mean the same thing for them. A verifier can fail to run, and "found nothing" must be distinguishable from "did not look". An object with a mandatory `status` field carrying exactly one of `ok`, `off`, `unavailable`, `timeout`, `unauthorized`, and a `findings` array that is meaningful only when `status` is `ok`, makes that distinction branchable; a bare array cannot express it.

The extract-then-compare pipeline should remain selectable despite losing the measurement, because it holds one property the winner cannot have and that property is about auditability rather than accuracy: its findings are re-derivable by anyone holding the two extracted records, with no model in the loop, whereas the direct comparison's findings are not re-derivable without a model. Its accuracy numbers (17/30 caught, 11/12 left alone) were taken on the earlier 14-case set and so are not comparable with the 15-case columns, which means the case for keeping it must rest on that property and not on its score.

The eval settles which approach to build and settles nothing about whether to build it. It settles the approach: on 15 cases run 3 times, the one-call direct comparison caught 32/33 planted defects and left 12/12 sound claims alone at $0.0060, against 28/32 and 7/12 at $0.0532 for the three-call extract-then-judge pipeline — better on both axes at a ninth of the cost, so the pipeline hypothesis did not survive measurement. It settles nothing about value, by its own statement: the case set is small, self-authored and synthetic with no case taken from a real memo, one case was found mislabeled by the model disagreeing with it, and "Nothing here measures whether warning an author earlier removes a grounding round, which is the actual cost argument."

The independence argument that rescued `Domain ⊆ Extent` transfers to a semantic mint-time verifier. `scope.rs` records that the comparison was abandoned as vacuous because one author supplying both sides produced byte-identical results about 80% of the time — "Independence, not capture, was what moved that number" — and that what fixed it was making one side captured by the tool (extent, with deliberately no flag to type one in) and the other authored (the note). A claim's proposition is authored by the same hand; its cited facts' captured output was recorded by `look`/`run` under the same no-typed-input rule. So the two sides of a proposition-versus-captured-output comparison are independent by the same construction, not by the author's diligence.

Rejected, each on its own measurement: a gate asked of the whole note (`whole`: -1% net on `fact`, 8% on `claim`); gate criteria rewritten for recall, dropping CHECK_SYSTEM's exclusions (`pick_recall`: 44% net on `fact` against `pick`'s 52%, and AUC 0.59 on `prose` against 0.65); the capture placed before the author's text (`pick_evfirst`: 20% net on `fact`); and a gate on `prose`, where no variant exceeds AUC 0.69. Also rejected without a run: surfacing any Jev probability to the author as a confidence, which `Finding` excludes by design.

findings.clause: no variant exceeds AUC 0.69
findings.why: The captured run reports AUCs for these sampled variants only. It does not establish the unrestricted claim that no variant outside this captured set exceeds 0.69.

prop: The environment-only rule for the API key needs one addition to `config.rs` and gets the rest for free. Shipping this falsifies one of `lib.rs`'s two pinned whole-crate properties, and the correct replacement is a per-command row rather than a weakened sentence — which is what the module's own preamble already prescribes, having recorded that "a single sentence about the whole crate was wrong for months" and having restated the write list per command for exactly that reason. The property that breaks is "there are no network calls anywhere, which the dependency set enforces rather than the prose": once an HTTP client is linked, the dependency set no longer enforces anything and the sentence would be prose pretending to be an invariant. The replacement row names the reaching commands — `fact`, `claim` and `prose` may make one outbound call to the configured provider, and only when enabled with a key in the environment — and states that `check`, `brief`, `query`, `review`, `workspaces`, `render`, `record` and `config` make none. The crate's other pinned property, that nothing here ever executes a command named by a document, is untouched and is the reason `check` must not be a reaching command.

The verifier's settings may be added to `config.rs` only because each is visible in the output it affects, which is the module's own stated admission test: "every setting here must be visible in the output it affects ... A setting that could not be shown that way should not be added to this file." The proposed `verify` result object satisfies it by echoing status, model name and the non-determinism marker in every response, so a reader can tell which settings produced the result in front of them without opening a config file. The keys — `verify.enabled` (bool), `verify.model` (string), `verify.approach` (direct or pipeline), `verify.timeout_ms` (int) and `verify.verbs` (which mint verbs are checked) — are each one entry in the existing static KEYS registry with an `accepts` rule, live at the two existing scopes, and need no third scope.

The extract-then-compare pipeline should remain selectable despite losing the measurement, because it holds one property the winner cannot have and that property is about auditability rather than accuracy: its findings are re-derivable by anyone holding the two extracted records, with no model in the loop, whereas the direct comparison's findings are not re-derivable without a model. Its accuracy numbers (17/30 caught, 11/12 left alone) were taken on the earlier 14-case set and so are not comparable with the 15-case columns, which means the case for keeping it must rest on that property and not on its score.

The warning should be carried as a top-level `verify` OBJECT in the mint result, not a fourth array beside `attention` and `overlap`. `mcp.rs` establishes the array form for a reason that holds here — "the caller is a program, and a field it can branch on beats a string it has to notice" — but `attention` and `overlap` are derived per call from workspace state already on disk, so empty and absent mean the same thing for them. A verifier can fail to run, and "found nothing" must be distinguishable from "did not look". An object with a mandatory `status` field carrying exactly one of `ok`, `off`, `unavailable`, `timeout`, `unauthorized`, and a `findings` array that is meaningful only when `status` is `ok`, makes that distinction branchable; a bare array cannot express it.

The eval settles which approach to build and settles nothing about whether to build it. It settles the approach: on 15 cases run 3 times, the one-call direct comparison caught 32/33 planted defects and left 12/12 sound claims alone at $0.0060, against 28/32 and 7/12 at $0.0532 for the three-call extract-then-judge pipeline — better on both axes at a ninth of the cost, so the pipeline hypothesis did not survive measurement. It settles nothing about value, by its own statement: the case set is small, self-authored and synthetic with no case taken from a real memo, one case was found mislabeled by the model disagreeing with it, and "Nothing here measures whether warning an author earlier removes a grounding round, which is the actual cost argument."

Latency is the binding constraint and it is larger than a per-record estimate suggests, because the unit that pays it is the tool call and not the record. In the largest memo on disk (tet47) the append-only logs carry 33 + 114 + 130 = 277 lines across facts, claims and prose, and 114 of those claim lines resolve to only 39 distinct claim ids — so roughly two thirds of claim traffic is revision. At the eval's observed per-call latency, verifying every line of that run costs tens of minutes of added wall-clock, while the money stays negligible. The design must therefore (a) commit the mint before the verifier runs, so a slow provider delays only the reply and never the record, (b) bound the wait with `verify.timeout_ms` and report `status: timeout` when it expires, and (c) skip the call entirely when a revision does not change the text being compared, which is where most of the volume is.

A workspace-local `verify.log` beside `refusals.log` is the right place for findings to persist, but `refusals.log` is the wrong sibling to imitate in one specific respect: it is an entry in SNAPSHOT_FILES and therefore ships into `<memo>.tetel/` with every render. A log of model output that shipped that way would put non-reproducible text into the snapshot, which is the one thing this design must not do. What makes the omission safe is that SNAPSHOT_FILES is an enumerated allowlist rather than a denylist — a new workspace file is withheld by default and ships only when someone adds a line with a justifying comment beside every other entry's. So `verify.log` is enforced out of the snapshot by construction, not by a promise, and its absence needs no new mechanism.

findings.clause: therefore ships into `<memo>.tetel/` with every render
findings.why: A render skips an absent `refusals.log`, so it does not ship that file with every render.

prop: The retrodiction test is runnable today on a corpus already on disk, and its shape is fixed by the file formats rather than chosen. Seven memos each carry an evidence log and a snapshot; the claim logs record Create and Revise events with a unix timestamp and the wording carried at each, so every claim's text as it stood at first render is reconstructible; the evidence logs are in-toto statements whose subject is a claim id and whose predicate carries a verdict. The denominators are known before the test runs, which is what makes a kill threshold statable in advance rather than negotiated afterwards.

The register that keeps a warning from reading as a refusal should ride in a per-finding `guidance` string, not only in the tool description. The precedent already does both: each `attention` entry carries a `guidance` value built beside the finding, and the surrounding tool descriptions set the tone in the same words — "It is not an error — read it and decide". Putting the sentence in the finding itself means it reaches a caller that never re-read the tool description, and it lands inside `fact_result`, the one builder this design already modifies, rather than requiring a separate edit that could drift from the payload. The `attention` precedent additionally shares its advice text verbatim with the CLI so the two surfaces cannot say different things about the same finding, and the `verify` guidance should be produced the same way.

prop: A finding must name the failing clause and quote the captured evidence rather than assert a verdict, and the eval supplies the reason as a measured case rather than a worry. The three-call pipeline's false positives were all one failure mode — the extractor drops a binding and the judge cannot tell a dropped binding from an absent one — and the recorded instance is a finding that reported "the evidence contains no `pin` name or binding" against evidence whose lines 425-436 are the pin computation. That finding is a verdict: a recipient can only accept or ignore it. Had it named the clause it was judging and quoted the evidence lines it judged against, its wrongness would have been visible in one step to a reader with the memo in front of them. So each entry carries the quoted clause, the fact id and the quoted span it was compared against, and no confidence score — the recipient is usually an agent that will act on a warning, and a verdict invites compliance where a quotation invites checking.

The register that keeps a warning from reading as a refusal should ride in a per-finding `guidance` string, not only in the tool description. The precedent already does both: each `attention` entry carries a `guidance` value built beside the finding, and the surrounding tool descriptions set the tone in the same words — "It is not an error — read it and decide". Putting the sentence in the finding itself means it reaches a caller that never re-read the tool description, and it lands inside `fact_result`, the one builder this design already modifies, rather than requiring a separate edit that could drift from the payload. The `attention` precedent additionally shares its advice text verbatim with the CLI so the two surfaces cannot say different things about the same finding, and the `verify` guidance should be produced the same way.

TET-28's "workspace-rooted" requirement is NOT decidable from today's capture in the case that matters most. When look_grep finds matches, it records one extent entry per matched file, keyed on that file's resolved path, with label "<file> (grep: <pattern>)" — and the search root appears nowhere in what is captured; the code's own comment says the entries are keyed "not by the search root or the grep command line". A repo-wide grep and a single-file grep that matched the same file therefore capture byte-identical extents. Every genuine census of a symbol an implementer is told to modify falls in this positive-match case, because the symbol's definition site matches.

The zero-match case IS decidable today, and it shows the shape the fix should take: a no-match grep records one entry whose key is the resolved search root and whose Marker { root, state } is resolved from that same root, so "was this bounded negative repo-wide" reduces to comparing two tool-captured strings on one entry — key versus world_root. TET-5's per-observation markers and the unconditional -H made this comparison meaningful; they did not extend it to the positive-match case.

The modification surface is small and censused. `fact_result` has exactly one definition and two production call sites, both in src/mcp.rs — the "minted" and "revised" arms — so adding a `verify` key to that one builder covers both fact outcomes and touches no other production caller; the only other occurrences in the worktree are a same-named local binding in a test. On the config side, `known_keys` occurs twice in the whole worktree, both inside src/config.rs, and `Accepts` six times, also all inside src/config.rs, with a single variant in use. Adding the `verify.*` keys therefore means new registry entries, new `Accepts` variants and matching arms in `accepted` and its message formatter, with no consumer outside that module to update.

The degradation contract is format-level and total: every terminal state of the provider call maps to exactly one `verify.status` value, and no state maps to `ok` with an empty `findings` array unless the model returned a well-formed answer containing no finding. Disabled by config gives `off`; no key in the environment gives `unauthorized`; a transport failure or non-2xx gives `unavailable`; expiry of `verify.timeout_ms` gives `timeout`. An empty or truncated response body is `unavailable` and never `ok`, because the eval measured exactly that state — a draw reaching the token ceiling returns a zero-length body — and because the same eval's harness recorded scoring an error as an answer as one of the two defects that inflated its own results. In every non-`ok` state the mint has already committed, so the contract can never fail a mint or change an exit code.

The retrodiction test is runnable today on a corpus already on disk, and its shape is fixed by the file formats rather than chosen. Seven memos each carry an evidence log and a snapshot; the claim logs record Create and Revise events with a unix timestamp and the wording carried at each, so every claim's text as it stood at first render is reconstructible; the evidence logs are in-toto statements whose subject is a claim id and whose predicate carries a verdict. Across all seven, 786 rows break down as 578 supports, 185 qualifies and 23 refutes — so the target set is the 208 non-supporting verdicts, and the measurement is: for each, was that claim's first-render wording one the verifier flags, and does the flag name the same defect the verdict named. The denominators are known before the test runs, which is what makes a kill threshold statable in advance rather than negotiated afterwards.

A census check cannot be built on labels, and the record model already shows the right way to extend the schema. At mint time only key, label, world_root and world_state survive into an ExtentEntry — the observation's kind is dropped, and the grep pattern exists only inside a display label, where an author-chosen pattern containing " in " or "(grep: " would make parsing ambiguous. The census therefore needs the new root-level search entry to carry two structured fields into ExtentEntry — the observation kind and the search pattern — following the exact precedent world_root set: #[serde(default)], with the empty value read as "predates the field, not eligible" rather than guessed about. Legacy facts can then never satisfy a census requirement, whose remedy is precisely to re-run the grep under the new capture. The snapshot already ships facts.jsonl with full extent entries, so check reads these fields from files every snapshot already contains; and because no surface lets an author supply an extent by hand, both sides of the rooting comparison and the pattern are tool-captured by construction.

The census therefore needs a small capture extension before any refusal can exist: look_grep should record, for every search, one root-level search entry — key = the resolved search root, a label carrying the pattern and the match-file count, marker resolved from the search root — alongside the existing per-file match entries, making the match and no-match cases uniform. "Workspace-rooted" then has one decidable definition covering both cases: the search entry's key equals its own world_root, a byte comparison of two strings the same look_grep call captured from the same canonicalized directory. No author-typed input participates on either side.

The decidable trigger is declaration (candidate 1): a modification target is a structured record the author creates — a symbol string plus a fact citation — and the refusal fires only on a declared target whose cited fact carries no qualifying census entry. This sits inside the machine partition's own stated principle, that machine failures are "objective contradictions between a document and the record it claims to rest on, decidable without a human": a target row is exactly a pointer at evidence, and "you did not point at your evidence" is the README's own example of a decidable question. The refusal's remedy is singular — run the workspace-rooted grep for that symbol, mint the fact, cite it (or withdraw the target) — so refusal rather than report is the right disposition for the declared-but-uncensused case, by the same discriminator under which scope.rs chose report: there, only a person can tell context from conclusion; here, nothing is left to tell.

Two results kill the feature, and both must be declared before the test is run. First, low recall against the verdicts that cost a round: if the verifier surfaces fewer than a quarter of the 23 refutes on their first-render wording, it does not catch the findings that force a revision round, and the whole cost argument — that warning earlier removes a grounding round — fails on the only corpus that could show it. Second, false-positive load: if the verifier flags more than one in ten of the 578 supporting claims at their first-render wording, it is a steering hazard, since the recipient is usually an agent that will act on a warning and each such flag is an invitation to damage a claim that was already sound. Either result kills it regardless of how the other lands, and a run that is merely disappointing on `qualifies` — the largest bucket at 185 — is not a kill, because a qualification is often a legitimate scope narrowing rather than a defect.

The rooting predicate — census entry's key byte-equals its own world_root — is satisfiable and fails closed. On this machine and repo the two spellings (fs-canonicalized search root; git rev-parse --show-toplevel) agree byte-for-byte, so an honestly rooted grep satisfies the predicate; and if the two tools ever disagree on spelling, the mismatch refuses an honest census loudly rather than accepting an unrooted one silently, because inequality can only ever deny rooting, never grant it. Two hardenings belong in the implementation: look_grep should itself compare the canonicalized search root against the marker's root at capture time and store the search entry's key in the marker's spelling when they name the same directory, so check stays a pure byte comparison; and the agreement should be pinned by a test, since one probe on one machine shows the common case, not an invariant.

A mention-triggered refusal (candidate 2) is off-charter and already measured dead in this repository. The charter forbids heuristic refusals outright, and scope.rs records the measurement: string-matching symbol references was tried for the note-outside-extent check and rejected because it "would have flagged a legitimate quotation ... while missing both real overreaches" — naming a symbol is normal, concluding about it is the failure, "and those two are not distinguishable by string matching". A refusal wired to that detector would refuse honest memos, which is precisely what scope.rs's "refusing would make the honest case unwritable" disposition exists to prevent. This also means the README Direction entry for this feature — "requiring a workspace-rooted search behind a claim that names a symbol" — is phrased as the mention-triggered shape and should be corrected to the declared-target shape when this ships.

No author-typed input participates on either side.

Latency is the binding constraint and it is larger than a per-record estimate suggests, because the unit that pays it is the tool call and not the record. In the largest memo on disk (tet47) the append-only logs carry 33 + 114 + 130 = 277 lines across facts, claims and prose, and 114 of those claim lines resolve to only 39 distinct claim ids — so roughly two thirds of claim traffic is revision. At the eval's observed per-call latency, verifying every line of that run costs tens of minutes of added wall-clock, while the money stays negligible. The design must therefore (a) commit the mint before the verifier runs, so a slow provider delays only the reply and never the record, (b) bound the wait with `verify.timeout_ms` and report `status: timeout` when it expires, and (c) skip the call entirely when a revision does not change the text being compared, which is where most of the volume is.

The refusal's remedy is singular — run the workspace-rooted grep for that symbol, mint the fact, cite it (or withdraw the target) — so refusal rather than report is the right disposition for the declared-but-uncensused case, by the same discriminator under which scope.rs chose report: there, only a person can tell context from conclusion; here, nothing is left to tell.

The rooting predicate — census entry's key byte-equals its own world_root — is satisfiable and fails closed. On this machine and repo the two spellings (fs-canonicalized search root; git rev-parse --show-toplevel) agree byte-for-byte, so an honestly rooted grep satisfies the predicate; and if the two tools ever disagree on spelling, the mismatch refuses an honest census loudly rather than accepting an unrooted one silently, because inequality can only ever deny rooting, never grant it. Two hardenings belong in the implementation: look_grep should itself compare the canonicalized search root against the marker's root at capture time and store the search entry's key in the marker's spelling when they name the same directory, so check stays a pure byte comparison; and the agreement should be pinned by a test, since one probe on one machine shows the common case, not an invariant.

The census's blind spots are boundable from what the capture actually does, and belong in check's printed non-coverage: (a) a textual grep cannot see dynamic dispatch, re-exports and aliased imports, or macro-generated and string-assembled identifiers; (b) the traversal is the system grep's — tetel deliberately shells out to it rather than reimplementing a dialect — so platform rules about symlinked directories and the -I binary skip bound what a "repo-wide" search physically visited; (c) rooting says where the search started, not which tree it should have been: whether the censused root is the tree the memo designs against stays with the reader, alongside the existing per-root tree-state report; (d) whether anyone read the census is the insincere-examination ceiling — capture makes the extent honest, not the interpretation; and (e) under-declared targets, by construction. The report mechanism for printing exactly this kind of standing limit already exists as the NON_COVERAGE list.

A census check cannot be built on labels, and the record model already shows the right way to extend the schema. At mint time only key, label, world_root and world_state survive into an ExtentEntry — the observation's kind is dropped, and the grep pattern exists only inside a display label, where an author-chosen pattern containing " in " or "(grep: " would make parsing ambiguous. The census therefore needs the new root-level search entry to carry two structured fields into ExtentEntry — the observation kind and the search pattern — following the exact precedent world_root set: #[serde(default)], with the empty value read as "predates the field, not eligible" rather than guessed about. Legacy facts can then never satisfy a census requirement, whose remedy is precisely to re-run the grep under the new capture. The snapshot already ships facts.jsonl with full extent entries, so check reads these fields from files every snapshot already contains; and because no surface lets an author supply an extent by hand, both sides of the rooting comparison and the pattern are tool-captured by construction.

Under-declaration — the memo recommends modifying a symbol it never declared — cannot be a refusal and must not be silently absorbed either. Deciding from prose that a sentence "tells an implementer to modify X" is a heuristic read of English, exactly the class the charter routes to the human-owed partition or nowhere; scope.rs's measured precedent shows the symbol-detector that trigger would need flags quotation and misses conclusion. The design therefore makes the omission visible instead of detected: (a) once a workspace declares any target, render emits a Modification targets section, and once any claim exists it emits the section even when empty — "Modification targets: none declared" — so a memo that recommends changes while declaring nothing shows a hole where the census should be, in front of every reader; and (b) check's standing non-coverage list, whose first entry is already "dependents that never declared themselves", gains a census-specific line ("a recommendation whose target was never declared") so the blind spot is printed rather than implicit.

The qualifying-census predicate, fully: a declared target (symbol S, citing fact F) is censused iff F's captured extent contains a search entry whose kind field says it is a whole-search record, whose pattern field byte-equals S, whose key byte-equals its own world_root, and whose world_root is git-backed (neither the no-git sentinel nor the empty predates-the-field value). Byte-equality of pattern to symbol is the only sound decidable comparison available: grep is invoked with the pattern verbatim (-e <pattern>), so a looser rule like "pattern contains the symbol" would accept a grep whose pattern merely embeds S in a longer string and therefore matches a strict subset of S's textual occurrences, while anything semantically wider would require deciding containment between regular expressions. Symbols that are not literal strings in the system grep's dialect are a stated limit of the census, not a case the check adjudicates.

The strictness objections to byte-level containment dissolve on the actual capture path, and every weaker relation reopens the invention channel. A donor comment wrapped across lines with interior prefix noise (`//`, `*`, indentation) IS a contiguous byte substring of a look_path capture, because look_path stores the file's bytes verbatim — the cost is only that the selected premise carries its comment syntax into the rendered section, which the "never paraphrase" constraint endorses rather than tolerates. Stripping that noise would require knowing each language's comment syntax, which is precisely the hard-coded per-language coupling scope.rs's "language-agnostic by construction" doctrine excludes. Two capture modes genuinely fight containment — grep-derived match outputs interleave "lineno:" prefixes between lines, and whole-search/no-match records carry empty output — so the design's guidance is that a donor fact is minted from `look` of the donor file; that is guidance about which observation to select from, not a new rule, since the relation is indifferent to which kind produced the bytes. Weaker relations fail: per-line containment lets an author stitch non-adjacent lines into a sentence the donor never wrote, and whitespace- or case-normalised matching means the memo shows text the capture does not contain — both are paraphrase with extra steps.

Where the refusal lives: at declaration, then re-verified at check. The `target` verb refuses to create a target whose cited fact carries no qualifying census entry — the same authoring-time shape as fact refusing on an empty pending buffer ("a fact needs a preceding look/run"; a target needs a preceding rooted census). Because a fact's extent is immutable once minted and a target is immutable once declared, this makes "every declared target is censused" a workspace invariant, and no render-path refusal is needed for workspace-authored documents; render's job is only to emit the targets section. check independently re-verifies the rendered document against its snapshot and reports [uncensused-target] as a machine failure in the partition's scope line, which is what catches a hand-authored or tampered document that never passed through the refusing verb. Like notes_outside_extent and mint_windows, that check runs only when a snapshot ships; without one, target rows are reported human-owed as unverifiable, consistent with the standing choice that a missing snapshot is human-owed rather than a machine failure. The verb must be one dispatch shared by CLI and MCP, the pattern look and fact already use, because this codebase has recorded a CLI/MCP drift on exactly such a duplicated act.

The ticket's trigger as written is undecidable in tetel's own record model, verified against the record types: a claim is only { id, proposition, cited fact ids, withdrawn }, a prose block only { heading, level, text, cited claim ids }, and nothing on either surface types a record as a recommendation or an instruction — prose creation is deliberately ungated because "prose is where the author talks, not where they're audited". So "a memo whose recommendation names a target" denotes no set of records any check can enumerate; any implementation of it would have to read English. The claim verb also supplies the refusal precedent the target verb extends: claim already refuses without --cites and on unknown fact ids, so "a structured record must cite a real record of the right shape" is the house's established authoring-refusal pattern.

"Transcribed verbatim" cannot be an honour-system field, and does not need to be: the decidable relation is that a premise's text is refused unless it is a verbatim substring of the cited donor fact's captured output. Both sides of that comparison are Strings the tool controls — a fact's output is produced only by look/run (file bytes read verbatim by look_path, grep match lines, a process's merged stream), no authoring surface lets anyone supply output by hand, and output is immutable after mint — so substring containment is a pure byte-level comparison with no normalisation step owned by the check. Typing is the selection mechanism, not the trust: the author types the premise, but a typed premise the donor never wrote fails containment and is refused at the verb. This is exactly the README's Direction item for supporting-span selection ("refused unless it is a verbatim substring of a cited fact — the author cannot type an extent, and here could not invent support, only select it"), and TET-29 is the first place it becomes load-bearing rather than roadmap.

TET-29's trigger must be a declaration, not a detection, by the same argument TET-28 implemented rather than merely designed. "Any design or fix that transplants a mechanism from another site" denotes no enumerable set of records: nothing in the record model types a claim or prose block as a transplant, and deciding from English (or from comparing code across two sites) that a fix "transplants" is a heuristic read — the class scope.rs measured dead for symbol mentions ("naming a symbol the code you read calls is normal; concluding about it is the failure; the two are not distinguishable by string matching") and the class targets.rs's shipped doc comment rules out as a refusal trigger. So a transplant is a record the author declares, the refusal attaches to the declaration, and under-declaration is handled the way TET-28 handles it: an always-rendered section that shows its hole, plus a printed non-coverage line, never a detector.

Containment against a fact's whole output has one genuine unsoundness, and it is fixable by the same schema move TET-28 already made. Fact.output is built at mint by joining the buffer entries' non-empty outputs with "\n", and the per-entry boundaries are not stored — so "substring of fact.output" can be satisfied by text straddling the seam between two observations: bytes that were never contiguous in anything the author actually saw, e.g. the tail of one file's capture concatenated with the head of another's. The fix is a serde-defaulted per-entry field on ExtentEntry recording the entry's output byte length, mirroring exactly how kind and pattern were added for TET-28: boundaries become reconstructible from lengths (skipping zero-length entries, matching the mint-time filter), the premise relation is then "verbatim substring of a single observation's output", and a donor fact minted before the field existed is ineligible with the same remedy TET-28 gives legacy facts — re-look and re-mint. Absent means not recorded, never guessed.

The transplant's destination should be a citation of a live modification target (T#), not a typed path and not an independent record — the two features compose. A transplant installs the donor's mechanism at a site the design necessarily tells the implementer to modify, so under TET-28's own rule that site should already be a declared target; making the transplant verb refuse a destination that is not a live target turns one declaration into a forcing function for the other, and narrows TET-28's admitted under-declaration blind spot for exactly the fix-shape that produced the motivating defect. The composition costs nothing at the edge cases: a green-field destination (new code, new symbol) is still censusable, because censuses() deliberately accepts a NoMatch search — "a symbol with no occurrences is censused by the grep that established it has none" — so declaring a target for a symbol that does not exist yet works today; and the destination-holds claims get a named, censused destination instead of a prose phrase. What the tool cannot verify — that the cited target really is where the mechanism lands — is content, and stays printed as non-coverage rather than guessed at.

The transplant record's shape follows from precedents already shipped, one field at a time. A transplant is an append-only record declared by a new verb (one dispatch shared by CLI and MCP, one new Kind variant and counter): (a) the donor is a citation of exactly ONE fact — the same single-citation rationale targets.rs states ("a target resting on 'one of these several facts' would leave which one undecided"), and a fact citation rather than a typed path because the donor site is then the fact's captured extent, which no author can type; (b) premise rows are verbatim selections from that donor fact's output (per C3-C5), immutable once selected — a selection of immutable bytes has nothing to revise honestly — and withdrawable with --why, mirroring target's withdraw-not-revise discipline; (c) a premise is discharged by citing a claim, in a separate later act, and because `tetel claim` refuses without --cites and on unknown fact ids, a discharge claim rests on at least one real fact by construction — the ticket's "must that claim itself rest on a fact?" is answered yes with zero new machinery; (d) a discharge can be superseded by a later discharge citing a different claim, append-only, so a refuted-and-replaced claim does not strand its premise.

An undischarged premise must be a legal workspace state, so the ticket's refusal cannot all move to the verb the way TET-28's did. The instrument works by transcribe-first: the author selects the donor's premises before knowing whether each holds at the destination — the confrontation the section exists to force. Refusing a premise row that cites no claim at declaration time would demand the destination-holds claim exist before the premise can be recorded, inverting that order (answer first, transcribe after) and pushing an author who cannot yet discharge a premise toward not declaring it at all — the same "refusing would make the honest case unwritable to catch the dishonest one" failure scope.rs's discriminator names. TET-28 never faced this because a census either exists or does not; a premise inventory is built across time. So the workspace invariant enforced at the verb is only "every premise is a genuine quotation of the cited donor's capture" (plus: donor fact exists and carries span boundaries, destination target exists and is live, a discharge cites an existing live claim); "every premise is discharged" is not a workspace invariant at all — it is a property of the finished document.

The transplant record's shape follows from precedents already shipped, one field at a time. An undischarged premise must be a legal workspace state, so the ticket's refusal cannot all move to the verb the way TET-28's did. The instrument works by transcribe-first: the author selects the donor's premises before knowing whether each holds at the destination — the confrontation the section exists to force. prop: The refusals land on three surfaces, each the earliest that can decide its own question. (1) At the verb: quotation invariants — donor fact exists and is span-eligible, premise text is a verbatim substring of a single observation's output, destination is a live target, a discharge names an existing live claim. These are per-record and decidable at creation, exactly like target's census refusal. (2) At `render --out`: completeness — a live transplant with an undischarged premise (none cited, or its discharge claim withdrawn) refuses the write. This is deliberately later than the verb (the intermediate state is legal while authoring) and deliberately earlier than check (the ticket's placement): --out is the act that writes the reviewable artifact and its snapshot under the pinned policy that a rendered memo is never hand-edited, so a memo with a declared-but-unexamined premise should fail to come into existence rather than exist and fail; the remedy is singular — discharge the premise, or withdraw it or its transplant with --why. A preview render (no --out) still assembles, marking undischarged rows loudly, so mid-work visibility is preserved; this render/--out asymmetry is new, and it is the design's most debatable departure. (3) At check: re-verification of everything above against the shipped snapshot — both directions, since tampering can go either way (a transplant row the snapshot lacks; a snapshot premise whose text is not contained in its donor fact's output; a premise whose discharge claim is withdrawn or missing) — as a machine failure in the same partition as uncensused targets, with rows in a snapshotless document reported human-owed as unverifiable, the standing choice for snapshot-dependent findings. Containment is re-checked byte-for-byte from facts.jsonl, which already ships full outputs; check runs nothing and fetches nothing to do it.

The containment relation was tested against the motivating case itself, at the source, and it passes — with one correction to the ticket's framing. The missed premise ("its parent is remote-known or was walked earlier in this same session", remote_utils.rs:4576 in lonic-forklift at HEAD) is contiguous bytes in a raw capture of the donor file, both as a single clause within one line and as the full seven-line `//` comment with its prefixes, so the verbatim-substring refusal admits it without any comment-syntax knowledge. But the premise does NOT live in the donor function's `///` doc block — collect_changed_closure's doc block never states the insert-before-check discipline or its ordering premise; both live only in the body comment below the signature. So the ticket's phrase "the donor's comment-stated premises" must not be operationalised as "the donor's doc block": the relation has to range over whatever bytes the author captured of the donor site, and a premise stated at a call site or in a body comment is selectable exactly when the author's donor fact folded an observation that covers it — the relation thereby pressures the author to capture the donor widely enough, and a known-but-uncaptured premise demands another look, not a typed row. Separately, today's repaired destination twin states the once-missed condition as one gradeable sentence ("Sound only parents-first — a child that marked a parent-explained hash would otherwise short-circuit the explaining parent's own audit"), which is concrete evidence that the discharge obligation this design demands — one claim per premise, stating that it holds at the destination — fits in a single claim proposition for the hardest observed case.

Every input the ticket names is present and travels with the memo: prose.jsonl and claims.jsonl ship inside `<memo>.tetel/`, each event in them carries a `timestamp: u64`, the prose→claim citation edges are the `cite` field of prose events, and a rendered ledger claim id is byte-identical to the workspace claim id. Two things the ticket does not name are also true and constrain the design: both loaders discard every timestamp, so the check must read the logs rather than the loaded types; and a prose block's own id is never written into the rendered document, so a residue line naming `P4` names something no reader of the memo alone can locate.

What the mechanism cannot catch is boundable and belongs in check's printed NON_COVERAGE list, which exists for exactly this ("a refusal that fired is easily read as coverage it never claimed"). Six entries: (a) a transplant the author never declared — no refusal can reach it; the empty section is its only trace; (b) premises the donor never wrote down — the relation selects from captured text, so a premise that lives in the donor's structure rather than its comments has nothing to select; (c) premises outside the captured extent — a donor fact that folded too narrow a look cannot yield a premise from the lines it never captured; (d) shallow selection — the tool verifies that selected bytes are the donor's, never that they are all the load-bearing ones; selecting one convenient clause and stopping is invisible to any format-level check, because deciding what counts as a premise is design judgment (the ticket says so) and deciding a selection is too small is a truth-check, the insincere-examination ceiling this project registered as permanently out of reach; (e) whether the discharge claim actually addresses its premise, and whether the cited target really is the mechanism's destination — both content; the claim is graded by a grounding pass as written, and the linkage is graded by nobody; (f) a donor comment that is itself wrong — verbatim quotation establishes provenance, never truth. None of these is reachable by a format-level refusal, so printing them is the honest disposition, not a fallback.

The mechanism's value is precisely that it moves one property across check's oldest declared blind spot, and grounding then does the rest. Per the ticket's account of the FORK-94 trail — recorded here as the ticket's report, not re-established — the defective remedy was graded supports twice, correctly, because the violated property was asserted by no claim at all; that situation is exactly the first entry in check's standing non-coverage list, "dependents that never declared themselves", and a grounder that grades propositions as written has nothing to grade where there is no proposition. Every piece of this design funnels toward converting that absent proposition into a present one: the premise row forces the donor's condition onto the page as captured bytes, and the discharge obligation forces a claim that the condition holds at the destination — a claim like any other, resting on facts by construction, entering the evidence ledger, graded by the next grounding pass, revisable and then out-of-proof until regraded. The tool never judges whether the claim is true; it refuses only the shape in which the question goes unasked. And the hardest observed case shows the converted claim fits in one sentence: today's repaired destination states the once-missed condition in a single doc-comment sentence, first-hand evidence that the discharge obligation is one gradeable proposition, not an essay.

The ticket's anchor — "revised since the last grounding pass" — would have gone silent on the finding the ticket cites. `brief::build` returns every ledger claim unconditionally, including already-grounded ones ("A claim leaves this list only by leaving the ledger itself — never by having been reported on"), so every subsequent pass re-grades a claim whose wording never changed and appends records with strictly later timestamps against the same digest. This is measured, not inferred: in the two shipped memos, tet28's C9 carries ten records on one unchanged digest from three passes spanning 1690 seconds, and tet28's C13 was graded `qualifies` by two passes 918 seconds apart on unchanged text. So an anchor at the *latest* grading advances past any fix-round prose edit as soon as one more pass runs — and the FORK-94 trail the ticket describes ran six rounds. The anchor must instead be the *earliest* record grading the claim's current wording: the moment that wording first entered proof, which a later pass over unchanged text cannot move.

findings.clause: every subsequent pass re-grades a claim whose wording never changed
findings.why: The captured output shows repeated grading for sampled claims and passes, but does not cover every subsequent pass, so the universal assertion is broader than the evidence.

The residue is about any prose whose text postdates the settling of what it cites, not about revision specifically: the block's timestamp is the one that set its current text, whether that was its `Create` or its last `Revise`, both of which carry a `timestamp` on the prose event. Including creations closes an identical exposure at near-zero cost in listings. It is identical because a paragraph written fresh under already-graded claims rests on them exactly as ungradedly as a rewritten one. It is near-zero cost because a paragraph created in a fix round to carry a new assertion normally cites a new claim, and a new claim is not in proof when the paragraph is written; by the time any pass has put it in proof, that first proof postdates the paragraph, so the block never becomes listable. What creation-counting does catch is the case worth catching: a new paragraph written under nothing but old, already-settled claims.

There is no digest-shaped alternative in the sharp sense, and the reason is structural rather than an omission: `out_of_proof` can compare digests because a record carries a digest of the very text it graded, whereas nothing in the record shape names or digests a prose block — not `Subject`, not `Predicate`, not `RecordInput` — and the grounding brief deliberately hands a pass only id, proposition and pin. Giving a record a prose digest would require the grounding pass to read the prose it is supposed to grade blind. A weaker, genuinely clock-free alternative is constructible: have `render --out` append a publication record — per prose block its text digest, per claim its proposition digest and whether anything grades it — so the residue becomes an ordinal comparison between successive publications with no clock anywhere. It is rejected on resolution, not on cost. A publication log samples state only at the renders the author happens to perform, so a prose edit and the grading that preceded it inside one publication interval are indistinguishable, and the FORK-94 shape — grounding pass, then fix-round prose, then one render — falls entirely inside a single interval and would be missed. The timestamp comparison resolves exactly that ordering, which is why it is worth its stated bound.

prop: Declaring this design's own modification targets took six whole-worktree searches — `check_file`, `prose_after_proof` and `block_offsets` in one fact, `Findings`, `NON_COVERAGE` and `render` in another — and measured a cost of the census mechanism that compounds with each memo the repository accumulates. A census is a whole-worktree search whose entire output is captured into a fact and shipped in the snapshot; in this repository the two previous memos' snapshots hold whole file dumps on single JSON lines, up to 57110 bytes each, so a search for a symbol this crate discusses re-captures those dumps. The measured weight for the four of the six symbols that already exist: `render` 486 matching lines and 405019 characters, `NON_COVERAGE` 35 lines and 98828 characters, `Findings` 23 lines and 59.2 KB, `check_file` 5 lines and 285 bytes; the two green-field symbols have no occurrences at all and are censused by the searches that established that. Two consequences follow. The largest captures exceeded what the authoring surface would return, so those symbol populations were established by the search while their individual sites went unread by the author — the census establishes rooting and extent, never that anyone looked at each site, which is a thing the census's own printed non-coverage already says in a different form. And the cost grows: every memo added to `docs/design/` enlarges the next memo's census of any symbol it discusses.

prop: The relative label must be derived from the canonicalized key against the entry's own world_root, never by stripping a prefix from the caller's spelling. Deriving it from the key makes the escape cases refuse automatically — the key is not under the repo root, so no strip applies and the label stays absolute — whereas a textual strip of the caller's spelling would mint `link/x.txt` for a file outside the repository.

A forgery surface exists and it is in the label, not the key. Measured on the current build: `look <repo>/link/x.txt` through a symlink out of the repo, and `look <repo>/../outside/x.txt`, both store a label textually beginning with the repo root while the file is outside it. In every such case the key — which is canonicalized — is the outside path, and the entry's own world_root is either `no-git-worktree` or the outside file's own repository, never the repository the label appears to sit under.

findings.clause: the entry's own world_root is either `no-git-worktree` or the outside file's own repository, never the repository the label appears to sit under.

prop: Declaring this design's own modification targets took six whole-worktree searches — `check_file`, `prose_after_proof` and `block_offsets` in one fact, `Findings`, `NON_COVERAGE` and `render` in another — and measured a cost of the census mechanism that compounds with each memo the repository accumulates. A census is a whole-worktree search whose entire output is captured into a fact and shipped in the snapshot; in this repository the two previous memos' snapshots hold whole file dumps on single JSON lines, up to 57110 bytes each, so a search for a symbol this crate discusses re-captures those dumps. The measured weight for the four of the six symbols that already exist: `render` 486 matching lines and 405019 characters, `NON_COVERAGE` 35 lines and 98828 characters, `Findings` 23 lines and 59.2 KB, `check_file` 5 lines and 285 bytes; the two green-field symbols have no occurrences at all and are censused by the searches that established that. Two consequences follow. The largest captures exceeded what the authoring surface would return, so those symbol populations were established by the search while their individual sites went unread by the author — the census establishes rooting and extent, never that anyone looked at each site, which is a thing the census's own printed non-coverage already says in a different form. And the cost grows: every memo added to `docs/design/` enlarges the next memo's census of any symbol it discusses.

prop: grep does not implement the ticket's first constraint — "an explicitly named path must still be read; only traversal skips" — and delegating that constraint to grep's flags would silently break it. Measured on BSD grep 2.6.0-FreeBSD: a file named explicitly on the command line is skipped when `--exclude` matches it (no output, exit 1, against output and exit 0 for the identical command without the flag), and a directory named explicitly as the recursion root is skipped when `--exclude-dir` matches it (same contrast). Only one of the three cases behaves the way the constraint describes: `--exclude-dir` does not suppress a file inside an excluded directory when that file is named explicitly and searched non-recursively.

A fact minted under the old behaviour therefore keeps the extent and pin it was minted with, whatever a later `look` would now do.

The ticket's headline reframing — that census output cost "~135k tokens, roughly 40% of the designer's reported 336k run" — is not reproducible from this design's evidence, and this run produced a direct counter-instance rather than merely failing to confirm it. `look_grep`'s return is genuinely uncapped in tetel: `printed.push_str(&stdout)` copies the grep's whole stdout into what `LookOutcome` hands back, with no length check, truncation or configuration between them. But when this design took a real whole-worktree census, the client harness rejected the 707,751-character result and returned roughly 1,300 characters of error text naming a spill file instead. So a large census's bytes need not enter a model's context at all, and the uncapped return does not by itself establish any figure in tokens. Two things remain true and are worth more than the figure: the bound that fired belongs to the caller rather than to tetel, and a different caller will not supply one; and nothing in `look_grep` records that anything downstream bounded what it returned, so a truncation leaves no trace in the fact it was minted into.

Capping what a fact stores and capping what a `look` returns are already separable in practice, and only the return path currently has any cap at all — imposed downstream, not by tetel. Taking this design's one census, `look --grep look_grep` rooted at the tetel worktree, the search succeeded and was recorded, but the agent harness refused to return the result, reporting 707,751 characters across 38 lines as exceeding its maximum allowed tokens and spilling it to a file; the author therefore never read the output of their own census, while the full captured output was nonetheless minted into the fact and ships in the snapshot. The census's own extent shows why: of the ten files matched, eight are tetel's own output — three snapshot `facts.jsonl`, one snapshot `claims.jsonl`, one snapshot `prose.jsonl`, two evidence ledgers and one rendered memo — and two, `src/observe.rs` and `src/worldstate.rs`, are source.

TET-28's census predicate needs no change, and this is what makes the two disclosures divide cleanly. `ExtentEntry::censuses` reads exactly five things — that the kind is `Search` or `NoMatch`, that the pattern byte-equals the symbol, that `world_root` is non-empty and not `NO_GIT`, and that `key == world_root` — and never reads `label` or `output`. A worktree-rooted search therefore still censuses after this change, correctly, because the predicate was always about a search's existence and rooting rather than about what it found. What changes is not the predicate but what a passing census entitles a reader to conclude, and that is carried by text: a standing line in `check` saying the exclusion policy exists, and the search record's own `label` saying which patterns this particular search was given.

"No `look` returns tetel's own content" is not the honest name for what this design builds, and the honest name is better rather than merely narrower: a `look` returns tetel's own output only when the caller named it. `look_path` refuses a directory and reads exactly the one file it was given, with no traversal of any kind, so every file it can ever return is one the caller named explicitly and it is left unchanged by this design. `look_grep` is where the whole mechanism lands, and its rule is the same sentence applied to a search — the exclusions are passed only when the root is a directory that is not itself tetel content, so what they remove is only ever reached by traversal. Stating the guarantee over naming rather than over `look`'s two modes covers both with one sentence and does not promise a reader something `look_path` never did.

A directory containing nothing but tetel's output is still not "explicitly named", and the cost of that is concrete rather than theoretical. `docs/design` holds exactly nine entries — three rendered memos, three evidence ledgers, three snapshot directories — and nothing else. A search rooted there for the symbol `census` returns 184 lines and 1,200,881 bytes today; under this rule it returns nothing and exits 1. The alternative, treating a directory as named when everything beneath it happens to be tetel's, is a judgement about a directory's contents rather than a test on a path, and the project rules that out as a refusal trigger. So the exclusion stays a format test on the root itself, and the price is that searching across memos requires naming a memo file or a snapshot directory rather than the folder they sit in.

The explicit-path exception must be implemented as a decision about whether to pass exclusion flags at all, and `look_grep`'s existing shape already supplies the discriminator. `look_grep` adds `-r` only when `root_path.is_dir()`, and passes `root` through to grep verbatim as the caller spelled it, never canonicalized. So the rule is: when the root is not a directory the caller has named a single file explicitly, and no exclusion flag is passed — which is required, since `--exclude` otherwise suppresses a file named on the command line. When the root is a directory that is itself tetel content, again no exclusion flag is passed — which is required, since `--exclude-dir` otherwise suppresses a directory named as the recursion root. A root counts as tetel content by three format tests and no others: some component of it ends with the literal `.tetel`, or its filename ends with `.evidence.jsonl`, or a directory named by appending `.tetel` to it exists. Only in the remaining case, a directory root that is not itself tetel content, are the three exclusions passed, and each must be spelled the way grep will construct the matched file's name from that same root string.

findings.clause: records exist, all with a digest differing from `sha256_hex(claim.proposition)`
findings.evidence:
let (fresh, stale): (Vec<&&EvidenceRecord>, Vec<&&EvidenceRecord>) = records
            .iter()
            .filter(|r| !r.proposition_digest.is_empty())
            .partition(|r| r.proposition_digest == current);
findings.why: Records with an empty digest are excluded from both partitions. Thus a claim can have a differing nonempty digest plus an empty-digest record and still be placed in `out_of_proof` when `fresh.is_empty()`, even though not all records have a differing digest.

prop: Every evidence record already stores a pin — on the witnessed path the pin of the grounder's own fact, i.e. the tree it stood in, written expressly so that "was this claim graded against the same tree the memo was written against?" becomes measurable — in a field no check reads today; so rule 3 is implementable as a comparison of that stored pin against the claim's currently stated pin, answerable on ledgers already written, whereas folding the pin into `sha256_hex` would change every pinned claim's current digest and drive every previously written record into `out_of_proof`.

No opt-out flag should be added, because three escape hatches already exist and each is reached by naming something rather than by setting a flag. `look_path` opens any single named file, including one inside a snapshot, and is untouched by this design. `look --grep` rooted at a path that is itself tetel content passes no exclusions at all, which is not merely permitted but forced: grep's `--exclude-dir` suppresses a directory named as the recursion root, so the flags must be withheld there or naming a snapshot directory would return nothing. And `run` spawns `argv` directly with nothing between the empty-argv refusal and the spawn that inspects, parses or classifies the command or the paths it will touch, so it has no place a path exclusion could be applied even in principle. The pin's non-stationarity is relocated rather than removed, and the relocation is the improvement. Measured on a scratch tree: rendering a second memo into it, changing no source, left the matched output of a search for the same symbol byte-identical while changing the emitted exclusion list from one rendered-memo pattern to two. So the captured output is now stationary against tetel's own churn — which was the ticket's within-run complaint, since an evidence ledger growing during grading no longer reaches the search at all — but the exclusion set is not, and because the design writes that set into the search record's label and the label is inside the pin, two censuses of the same symbol against the same source will still pin differently across a render. The difference is that the cause is now written in plain text in the same record, instead of being an invisible change in what the search happened to read.

There should be no `--owed` flag: because the full brief is emitted either way, an owed section is purely additive and there is no prior behaviour a flag would preserve, while TET-46's stated objection to a flag — that it "leaves no trace in what the caller named, only in how they configured the call" — applies with more force to a brief, the one artifact independence rests on, since two passes running `brief` on the same memo would otherwise receive different documents; the confirmation floor stays a parameter, and the value in force is printed in the brief so that this piece of configuration does leave a trace in the artifact.

The donor's exclusion of ledger claims rests on two properties the owed closure does not share — a ledger claim "cannot be a cascade root (no typed `Status`)" and is not a `Row`, so cannot be a row→row dependent — whereas the owed closure roots at owed-ness under rules 1-4, which is defined for a ledger claim and for nothing else, and its dependents are ledger claims by construction; so the exclusion does not carry across, and the index is built over precisely the population the donor omitted.

Rule 4's visibility requirement is met by extending the existing per-claim provenance line in `grounding_provenance` with the number of distinct non-author workspaces that graded the claim's current wording, printed as a bullet in the human-owed partition exactly as that line already is; `check` states the count and never compares it against a floor, because the floor is `brief`'s parameter and a comparison printed by `check` would be a per-claim verdict on a policy setting rather than a count of records.

The donor's self-citation exclusion is not needed at the destination: check 5 skips a self-edge so that a root is "never reported as its own dependent", whereas the owed closure's output is a set of ids to grade that already contains its own seeds, so a self-edge can only re-derive owed-ness a claim already has and changes neither the set nor its termination.

prop: The `prose-revised-since-proof` listing is a pure function of three recomputed quantities and stores none of them: a block's current (text, cite-list) pair, the timestamp at which that exact pair first appeared in the block's event history, and an anchor equal to the maximum over the block's cited claims of each claim's earliest non-refuting record whose proposition digest matches the claim's current wording. The block is listed exactly when the pair's first-appearance timestamp exceeds the anchor, and is skipped outright when it is a heading, when its current cite-list is empty, or when no cited claim has such a record.

The acknowledgement event cannot live in `prose.jsonl`. `ProseEvent` is an internally-tagged serde enum over exactly `Create` and `Revise`, and `workspace::read_jsonl` propagates any line's parse failure as an error over the whole log rather than skipping it; empirically, a build at this pin reading a `prose.jsonl` containing one valid `Create` line and one `{"event":"Ack",...}` line fails the entire read with `unknown variant \`Ack\`, expected \`Create\` or \`Revise\`` and exits 1. A new tag value therefore makes every older build unable to read even the prose it already understood.

prop: The `prose-revised-since-proof` listing is a pure function of three recomputed quantities and stores none of them: a block's current (text, cite-list) pair, the timestamp at which that exact pair first appeared in the block's event history, and an anchor equal to the maximum over the block's cited claims of each claim's earliest non-refuting record whose proposition digest matches the claim's current wording. The block is listed exactly when the pair's first-appearance timestamp exceeds the anchor, and is skipped outright when it is a heading, when its current cite-list is empty, or when no cited claim has such a record.

Recording "showed N of M" in the label does not violate the crate's "nothing derived is stored" rule. That rule is stated as a reason to recompute values a re-run can obtain from the shipped ledger, and the shown-count is not one of them: the `Search` entry's `output` is empty and the per-file entries record what was captured, not how much of it was returned, so how much the author was shown is unrecoverable from the ledger after the fact. It is an event, and recording it is the only way it survives.

The sketch's second suppression clause — that the ack's timestamp be later than the recomputed anchor — is dropped, because it cannot fire. The rule is only consulted for a block the trigger already listed, and listing means the current pair's first-appearance timestamp already exceeds the anchor; an ack recording that same current pair is appended to an append-only log by the same authoring workspace, after that pair exists, and stamped by the same `workspace::now_unix()` that stamped the prose event. So unless the authoring machine's clock runs backwards between the two appends, the ack's timestamp exceeds the block timestamp which already exceeds the anchor, and the clause is satisfied in every case it is evaluated. Dropping it leaves the suppression predicate free of any timestamp comparison at all, which is why — unlike the trigger it guards — the acknowledgement does not rest on two clocks agreeing.

The acknowledgement is a strict filter over the trigger's output, applied after `prose_after_proof` has produced its list, and therefore cannot add a listing that TET-30 would not have produced — a stale, malformed or unmatched ack simply fails to suppress, which is the same state as no ack at all. Two consequences hold without further argument: the set of blocks the reader is asked to act on is always a subset of TET-30's, so no new false demand can be manufactured; and `machine_check_failed` is untouched, since `prose_revised_since_proof` is not among its disjuncts and the ack changes only which entries populate it. It also follows that the digest component does not close any part of TET-30's conceded non-coverage for prose that ships alongside a claim revision — it only stops an acknowledgement outliving the state it attested to.

For a claims-unaffected prose edit — a typo or wording fix that leaves every cited claim's proposition untouched — both of TET-30's two clearing acts misrepresent what the author did. Restoring the text and citation list, which C6 names as the first act, restores the defect the edit corrected. Revising or adding a cited claim and having the new wording graded, C6's second act, requires changing a claim that is correct; and because `out_of_proof` is one of the disjuncts of `Findings::machine_check_failed` while `prose_revised_since_proof` is not, that route drives the run to a machine failure until a further grounding pass lands, spending a red check and a pass to silence a line that never failed the run.

An acknowledgement must not enter `render`'s output. Keeping the rendered bytes a function of facts, claims, prose, targets and transplants only — with `acks.jsonl` shipped by the snapshot copy loop but never read by `compose::render` — preserves the determinism the provenance-drift finding rests on, and buys a property that makes the required re-render honest rather than merely tolerable: re-rendering after an ack and nothing else rewrites the snapshot in place, since existing snapshot files are overwritten, while leaving the memo byte-identical. The discharge therefore shows up in version control as a change to the record and no change to the argument, which is exactly what it is.

The acknowledgement is an event in `acks.jsonl` recording five things — the block id, the block's current text, its current citation list, the sha256 digest of each cited claim's proposition **as `claims.jsonl` holds it**, and a verbatim `--why` — plus the `workspace::now_unix()` timestamp every workspace event carries. A listing is suppressed if and only if some ack for that block records a text, citation list and set of cited-claim proposition digests all equal, byte for byte, to the ones the check recomputes for that block at check time, with the digests recomputed from the snapshot's `claims.jsonl` — the same source the ack was minted from, and deliberately not the ledger-derived propositions the in-proof test must use, since the two are not the same string and a claim whose proposition carries an embedded newline or edge whitespace would otherwise be unackable with nothing red to say so. The predicate is pure equality over recomputed values; nothing derived is stored.

Three invalidation invariants follow from the key, each with the mutation that reddens its test. (i) Any later change to the block's text or to its citation list voids the ack, because both are components of the key; the mutation is to compare only the text, after which a citation-only revision — which TET-30's C6 records as an act that lists rather than clears — would stay suppressed. (ii) Any change to a cited claim's proposition voids the ack, because the key carries that claim's proposition digest; the mutation is to drop the digest set from the key, after which an ack would outlive a rewrite of the very claim the author read the paragraph against. (iii) A workspace with no `acks.jsonl` produces byte-identical output to today's, because `workspace::read_jsonl` treats a missing file as an empty log rather than an error; the mutation is to make the missing file an error, after which every memo rendered before this design existed would fail to check.

prop: Two entries are owed in `NON_COVERAGE`, by the list's own stated standard that a deliberate exclusion earns its own line because a refusal that fired is easily read as coverage it never claimed. First: that an acknowledgement records only that a human said they re-read the paragraph against its claims, and that nothing verifies the reading happened or judges whether the paragraph is faithful — the tool's silence after an ack is the author's assertion, not the tool's finding. Second: that an acknowledgement minted after the last `render --out` is not in the snapshot the check reads, so it does not suppress anything until the memo is re-rendered. Both are static general statements, which is the only form entries in this constant can take.

The minting surface is one verb, `tetel prose --ack <id> --why <text>` with the matching MCP argument pair, built as a variant of the single request shape both front ends already share so the two cannot drift on which missing flag is refused. Both are static general statements, which is the only form entries in this constant can take.

The design's contribution is therefore to print the block's cited claim ids beside that verbatim reason in the acknowledged bullet, so a reader can pair the author's own words to the citations, and to leave the non-coverage entry standing.

findings.clause: records exist, all with a digest differing from `sha256_hex(claim.proposition)`
findings.why: `out_of_proof` is populated when `fresh` is empty, but `fresh` and `stale` are partitioned only after records with an empty digest are filtered out.
